newsitem.title: THAILAND: Karen rebel chief Bo Mya fights for survival.
newsitem.headline: Karen rebel chief Bo Mya fights for survival.

text.p: Burma's rebel Karen National Union (KNU) leader Bo Mya is using Karen refugees as a human shield to buy time to try to avert a looming split within his ranks, rebel and Thai border officials said on Tuesday.

The KNU, one of the world's oldest rebel organisations still fighting a government, may be near the brink of collapse because of serious policy differences between the hardline General Bo Mya and moderate vice president Swe Seing, they told Reuters.
Their rift has created uncertainty among more than 70,000 Karen refugees who have been camping along Thailand's western border with Burma since 1984.

It has also cast a pall over more than 20,000 other Karen refugees who arrived in Thailand after fleeing fighting last week between Burmese troops and KNU guerrillas inside eastern Burma, the sources said.

Burmese troops destroyed several key KNU mobile camps inside their soil which ruffled rebel ranks and led to charges by some that Bo Mya's hardline stance led to the guerrilla group's recent string of setbacks.

The predominantly-Christian KNU was formed in 1948 to fight for greater autonomy from Burma's central government. It was wracked by a major internal split in 1994 and lost all bases and headquarters on the Burma side in March 1995.

But it is still one of the last holdouts among Burma's dozen ethnic rebel groups, most of which have recently signed peace pacts with Rangoon after having fought the central government on and off since the country's independence from Britain.

Bo Mya, 71, KNU head since 1976 but now leader of a smaller group of guerrillas, has vowed to fight the ruling Burmese State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) and refused to lay down arms despite Rangoon's peace offers.
He was not available for comment.
But a more moderate and powerful faction lead by KNU vice president, General Swe Seing, want to soften their stance and start some negotiations for peace with Burma, KNU sources said.

"The KNU is about to collapse because of the internal conflict. That is why a certain group of people who are very selfish have decided to use the civilians as the shield for survival," said a top KNU official who declined to be named.
The official said he was referring to Bo Mya and his loyalists as the group of people fighting for survival.
"He (Bo Mya) was supposed to be finished since (1995) and be replaced by Swe Seing but the old man is too selfish and people are too scared of him," he added.
He estimated that 70 percent of KNU guerrillas who used to be under Bo Mya were either living in Thai border towns or mingling with the refugees in the camps.

Some KNU guerrillas had taken the opportunity of reports of Burmese attacks on their mobile camps and tensions that followed to join in the new influx of refugees and live under the patronage of international aid agencies, he added.
"We have nothing left now. No forests, the Burmese are everywhere, and so the only place to live and survive in are refugees camps in Thailand," a senior KNU official said.

The Burma-backed Democratic Karen Buddhist Army (DKBA), which caused the KNU split in 1995, has accused KNU guerrillas of hiding in refugee camps and sneaking out to launch surprise sabotage and attacks on them inside Burmese soil.
Reports of more heavy Burmese-KNU fighting and high border tension after last week's Rangoon attack on KNU positions were exaggerated, Thai border and KNU sources said.
"It is true that there is not much fighting on the border but the news on presence of Burmese troops near the border always makes people scared," said Ma Tha, a senior KNU leader.
Burma has vowed to clear out all KNU guerrillas from its eastern border, saying they posed a major security threat.
